newsitem.title: USA: G7 seen opening door for additional dollar gains.
newsitem.headline: G7 seen opening door for additional dollar gains.

text.p: Currency markets are likely to push the dollar to fresh peaks in coming weeks following a Group of Seven communique on Sunday which failed to voice dissatisfaction with present exchange rate levels.
Analysts and traders said the absence of such language should open the door for additional dollar gains.

"They clearly are not worried about the level of the dollar at the present time though they are worried about how fast it could accelerate," said Bob Savage, chief foreign exchange dealer at Lehman Brothers.

In stressing the need to avoid currency fluctuations which spur trade imbalances and calling excess volatility undesirable, the lengthy joint statement -- issued after talks between G7 finance ministers and central bankers -- went beyond a statement issued last February in Berlin.

But the communique itself did not make any explicit reference to dollar strength or yen weakness, nor did it suggest that active intervention from the German, Japanese or U.S. central banks was imminent.
"This basiscally makes people comfortable with the idea we will see 1.80 in dollar/mark and 130 in dollar/yen," Savage said.

In the immediate aftermath of the communique's release, the dollar pushed as high as 1.7389 marks, its highest level in over three years, and above 127 yen, just shy of a four-and-a-half year peak of 127.19 touched earlier this month.
Ahead of the Sunday gathering, currency market participants had feared tougher language to stop the greenback's rise.

The U.S. currency has risen by more than 50 percent against the Japanese yen over the past two years, boosting Japanese export competitiveness, but also leading to diminishing confidence in Japan's economy and asset markets.
The United States has worried openly about gains in Japan's trade surplus of late, fearing the Japanese are relying excessively on a weak yen and higher exports to generate growth.
The source of dollar strength -- and a reason G7 officials would find it difficult to counter -- has been an extremely supportive economic backdrop.

U.S. growth is robust and the market expects additional interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve in the months ahead. In contrast, European and Japanese interest rates are extremely low, reflecting sub-par growth in these regions.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said at a press briefing following the meeting that foreign exchange rates levels were appropriate and continued to reflect fundamentals.

He also noted that he believed the U.S. was interested in a strong dollar, but not a stronger dollar. Whether the U.S. is ready to prevent a stronger dollar and risk sending it lower, however, is questionable after Sunday's communique.
"It's hard for the G7 to stop the dollar on basis of economic fundamentals, which are still very positive," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc.
"The risk of intervening and driving the dollar down and that getting out of control is too big a risk at this point in time."
Economists said key U.S. data on employment, growth and manufacturing activity due this week is expected to be robust -- an outcome which would add additional fuel to the dollar fire.
Expect traders to keep a keen eye of U.S.-Japan bilateral trade numbers in the months to come. Significant gains in Japan's surplus would keep the dollar capped, analysts said.
But in the absence of such developments, the market is likely to persist in pushing the greenback higher in order to test the tolerance limits of the G7.

"Trade is the only fundamental the G7 can point to that suggests the dollar could be overshooting," said David Gilmore, partner at advisory firm Foreign Exchange Analytics. "I think we will find the market testing if intervention is a possibility."
